title: YOUR BODY IS NOT YOUR OWN—SO WHY ARE YOU GIVING IT TO SOMETHING THAT IS DESTROYING YOU?
paragraphs: YOUR BODY IS NOT YOUR OWN—SO WHY ARE YOU GIVING IT TO SOMETHING THAT IS DESTROYING YOU?

Paul wrote six words that confront our most private compromises. But behind his warning about sexual sin is a breathtaking truth about the blood of Jesus, the value of your body, and the grace that can rewrite even the chapters you are most ashamed to remember.
There is a version of you that everybody sees.
The one who smiles in photographs. Goes to church. Shares Bible verses. Says “God bless you” without thinking twice.
And then there is the version of you that sometimes appears when nobody is watching.
When the room is quiet.
When the phone is in your hand.
When loneliness starts whispering.
When an old relationship sends a message.
When the desire to feel wanted becomes louder than the conviction you felt during Sunday worship.
And somewhere between what you know is holy and what your flesh desperately wants, a battle begins that nobody else can see.
Maybe you have won that battle a hundred times.
Maybe you lost it last night.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret you have promised God you would never repeat.
The most devastating part of sexual sin is not merely that you broke a rule. It is that you have forgotten how precious you are to the One who purchased you.
And the apostle Paul understood that truth so deeply that he wrote words capable of shaking the foundations of how we see our bodies, our desires, our relationships, and our salvation.
“Ye are not your own. For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.”
— 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, King James Version
Read that again.
Ye are not your own.
Not because your body is worthless.
Not because God despises human desire.
Not because Christianity teaches that sexuality is dirty.
But because something happened at Calvary that changed the meaning of your existence forever.
And to understand what Paul was really saying, we need to return to a city where sexual compromise was not unusual.
It was normal.
Corinth was a wealthy, culturally diverse Roman city where believers were learning to follow Jesus in a society with very different assumptions about sex, status, freedom, and the human body.
Some Christians had apparently begun treating bodily appetites as though they were spiritually insignificant.
Paul confronted that thinking directly.
“All things are lawful for me,” was a slogan he addressed in 1 Corinthians 6:12.
But his response exposed the danger of confusing freedom with permission.
“All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient.”
And then he added something that should make every believer examine the habits they have learned to excuse.
“I will not be brought under the power of any.”
In other words, Christian freedom is not permission to become enslaved.
You can call something harmless while it is quietly mastering you.
You can insist that you are in control while arranging your entire private life around the next opportunity to satisfy a craving.
You can tell yourself, “I can stop whenever I want,” while repeatedly discovering how difficult stopping has become.
And sometimes the most dangerous chains are the ones we have learned to decorate with excuses.
“It is just entertainment.”
“We love each other.”
“Everybody does it.”
“It is not hurting anybody.”
“God knows my heart.”
Yes.
God knows your heart.
He knows the loneliness beneath your decisions.
He knows the wounds you never explained.
He knows the affection you were desperate to receive.
He knows the moments when you confused being desired with being loved.
But knowing your pain does not mean He will call destructive choices good.
Jesus loves you too much to leave you enslaved to what is slowly consuming you.
Paul takes his argument further in 1 Corinthians 6:15.
“Know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ?”
Pause there.
Your body.
Not merely your thoughts.
Not only your prayers.
Not just your Sunday worship.
Your physical body belongs within your relationship with Jesus Christ.
Paul then speaks specifically about sexual union, explaining that becoming joined to a prostitute is not spiritually meaningless. He cites Genesis 2:24: “they two shall be one flesh.”
This is why his warning cannot be reduced to religious embarrassment about sex.
Scripture presents sexual union as profoundly significant.
God created human beings as embodied creatures. He created sexuality, and within His design for marriage, sexual intimacy is a good gift rather than something shameful.
But a gift can be misused.
And when something designed to express covenant faithfulness becomes separated from God's purposes, it can leave behind wounds that pleasure alone cannot heal.

Not every painful relationship involved sexual sin. Not every sexual failure produces the same consequences. But Paul refuses to pretend that what we do with our bodies is disconnected from who we are before God.
Then comes the command in 1 Corinthians 6:18.
“Flee fornication.”
In the original Greek, Paul writes:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.
Pheugete tēn porneian.
The verb pheugete means “flee” or “run away.” It is a present imperative, communicating an ongoing command.
The noun porneia refers broadly to sexual immorality. In this passage, Paul is not merely condemning one particular act while approving every other sexual behavior outside God's design.
He is calling believers away from sexual immorality altogether.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say, “See how close you can get.”
He does not say, “Keep testing your strength.”
He does not say, “Stay in the situation until you feel spiritually powerful enough to resist.”
He says:
Flee.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is leave.
Delete the conversation.
End the secret arrangement.
Stop returning to the website.
Refuse the invitation.
Tell someone trustworthy what has been happening.
Get help when the pattern has become compulsive.
Not because running makes you weak.
Because wisdom recognizes danger before desire has finished negotiating.
Joseph understood something similar when Potiphar's wife attempted to seduce him in Genesis 39.
He did not remain to prove how disciplined he was.
He fled.
And there are moments when the doorway out of temptation is an answer to prayer you must actually walk through.
But here is where Paul's words become even more astonishing.
After commanding believers to flee sexual immorality, he asks:
“What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?”
— 1 Corinthians 6:19, KJV
The Greek text contains a phrase that deserves careful attention:
τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν
To sōma hymōn naos tou en hymin hagiou pneumatos estin.
A close rendering is:
“Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you.”
The word naos refers to a temple or sanctuary, particularly the sacred dwelling place associated with divine presence.
Paul is not telling Christians that their bodies have become gods.
He is saying something far more humbling.
The Holy Spirit dwells in believers.
The body is not disposable packaging for a supposedly more important soul.
It matters to God.
And because Paul is addressing the Corinthian church, the plural language also reminds us that holiness is not merely an isolated private project. Our lives are bound to Christ and to His people.
Think about that.
The body you sometimes criticize in the mirror.
The body that has grown older.
The body marked by scars.
The body that has endured sickness, rejection, exhaustion, or regret.
The body you may have used in ways you now wish you could undo.
For the believer, that body is not beneath God's concern.
It is included in His redemptive purpose.
And the Holy Spirit's presence is not a reward reserved for Christians who have never struggled.
He is God's gracious gift to those who belong to Christ.
That truth should produce reverence.
But it should also produce hope.
Because the God who calls you to holiness has not abandoned you to achieve it through sheer willpower.
He gives His Spirit to His people.
And that changes everything.
Now listen carefully, especially if your sexual history is something you have learned to hate yourself for.
Your past may explain some of your wounds, but it does not have the authority to cancel what Jesus accomplished on the cross.
Perhaps you crossed boundaries you once promised you would never cross.
Perhaps you gave yourself to someone who promised forever and disappeared when commitment became inconvenient.
Perhaps you stayed in a relationship because you feared nobody else would ever love you.
Perhaps you have struggled with pornography for years and are tired of making promises you cannot seem to keep.
Perhaps you were sexually abused or exploited.

If that last experience is yours, hear this clearly: what someone did to you was not your sexual sin. The responsibility belongs to the person who violated you. You do not need to repent for being harmed.
And whatever your history, your worth has never depended on your sexual experience, your relationship status, or your ability to present a spotless past.
The Gospel is not the announcement that only people with clean histories may approach God.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Paul had already reminded the Corinthians of this earlier in the same chapter.
After naming various sins, including sexual immorality, he wrote:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”
— 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
Do not rush past those words.
Such were some of you.
These were not imaginary people who had never made terrible decisions.
They were real believers with real histories.
People whose former lives included things the surrounding culture might have celebrated, tolerated, or concealed.
Yet Paul did not address them as hopeless cases.
He pointed to what God had done.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not by pretending sin was harmless.
Not by rewriting God's moral standards.
But through the saving work of Jesus Christ and the Spirit of God.
This is the scandal of grace.
The holy God who refuses to call evil good is the same God who welcomes repentant sinners through His Son.
Grace does not erase the seriousness of sin.
Grace reveals how serious sin is by showing us what our redemption cost.
And that brings us to the final words of Paul's argument.
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς
Ēgorasthēte gar timēs.
“For you were bought with a price.”
— 1 Corinthians 6:20
The verb ēgorasthēte comes from agorazō, meaning “to buy” or “purchase.”
Paul uses the language of purchase to describe the believer's belonging to God.
But we must be careful not to make the image say more than Scripture says.
Paul does not describe God as a cruel owner who purchases people for exploitation.
His point is that believers have been redeemed from their former bondage and now belong to the Lord who saved them.
And elsewhere Scripture makes the cost of that redemption unmistakable.
“Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold ... But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.”
— 1 Peter 1:18–19, KJV
There it is.
The price.
Not money.
Not human achievement.
Not a lifetime of religious performance.
The precious blood of Jesus Christ.
And suddenly Paul's words become intensely personal.
Your body is not your own because your life has been claimed by the Savior who gave Himself for you.
He was betrayed.
He was mocked.
He was scourged.
He was crucified.
And He willingly endured the cross to accomplish the salvation of His people.
The sinless Son of God bore sin's judgment, died, and rose again.
So when Paul says, “Glorify God in your body,” he is not handing believers a random collection of religious restrictions.
He is drawing a conclusion from redemption.
Because Christ has redeemed you, your body is to be used in ways that honor Him.
Not to earn the purchase.
But because the purchase has already been made.
And perhaps that is the truth your heart has been resisting.
You want Jesus to forgive your past.
But you are frightened of letting Him govern your present.
You want His comfort when your heart breaks.
But His commands sometimes confront the very relationships and habits you have used to comfort yourself.
You want freedom from guilt.
But part of you still wants to keep the thing producing it.
That conflict is real.
And the answer is not to pretend it disappears the moment someone becomes a Christian.
Believers still experience temptation.
They still need repentance.
They still need accountability, prayer, wisdom, and the renewing work of the Holy Spirit.
But the Gospel calls us to stop treating the grace of God as permission to remain unchanged.
Romans 6:1–2 asks whether Christians should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
Paul's answer is emphatic:
“God forbid.”
The grace that forgives also trains us to turn away from ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 teaches.
And here is something many wounded Christians desperately need to hear.
Temptation is not the same as surrender. Struggle is not the same as hypocrisy. And repentance is not the same as perfection.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet without sin, according to Hebrews 4:15.
If you are fighting temptation, do not conclude that the battle itself proves God has rejected you.
But do not mistake feeling guilty for genuinely turning around, either.
Repentance is more than crying after a failure.
It means turning from sin toward God.
It means bringing hidden behavior into the light.
It means accepting that some doors need to close even when your emotions beg you to keep them open.
It may mean ending an immoral relationship, seeking pastoral care, establishing practical boundaries, or receiving professional support when harmful patterns are deeply entrenched.
And when you fall, the answer is not to run farther into darkness.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise does not make sin insignificant.
It makes confession possible.
Because Jesus Christ is not surprised by the sin you are afraid to admit.
He already knows.
And the One who knows is the One who calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
Remember the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
Her accusers wanted condemnation.
Jesus exposed their hypocrisy and refused to join their attempt to destroy her.
Then He said:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
— John 8:11, KJV
Those two truths belong together.
Mercy.
And a call to a changed life.
Jesus did not tell her that sin was imaginary.
He also did not treat her as a person beyond hope.
He met her with mercy and called her away from sin.
That is the Savior we proclaim.
Not a Jesus who excuses everything.
Not a Jesus who delights in crushing the ashamed.
But the holy and merciful Lord who calls people out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And perhaps today that call is reaching into a place you have kept locked for years.
The relationship nobody knows about.
The private messages.
The images you keep returning to.
The bitterness that has convinced you genuine love is impossible.
The shame that makes you feel unworthy of prayer.
You do not have to describe those things publicly to prove you are sincere.
But you do need to stop believing that hiding them from other people means they are hidden from God.
And you need to know that coming into the light does not mean your story is over.
It may mean your healing is beginning.
Not all at once.
Not without consequences.
Not without difficult decisions.
But with the real hope of transformation through Jesus Christ.
And there is another truth we must not overlook.
Paul's command is not only for unmarried people.
It is not only for those struggling with pornography.
It is not only for people with scandalous histories.
It is for the whole church.

Sexual holiness includes faithfulness within marriage, honoring other people's dignity, refusing exploitation, rejecting coercion, and treating human beings as people made in God's image rather than objects for personal gratification.
Marriage does not give someone permission to violate another person's dignity or consent.
And singleness does not make someone spiritually incomplete.
Christ is sufficient for His people in every season.
Holiness is not a competition to see who can appear most respectable.
It is the daily surrender of our lives to the Lord who redeemed us.
So what does it look like to glorify God in your body?
It looks like refusing to use someone else's loneliness for your pleasure.
It looks like telling the truth when deception would be easier.
It looks like honoring your marriage vows.
It looks like practicing self-control when nobody would discover your compromise.
It looks like refusing to measure your worth by how many people desire you.
It looks like seeking help instead of allowing shame to keep you isolated.
And sometimes it looks like sitting alone at the edge of your bed, tears falling, and praying the most honest prayer you have spoken in years.
“Lord Jesus, I cannot keep pretending. I need Your forgiveness. I need Your strength. Teach me to love what is holy. Help me turn away from what dishonors You. I belong to You.”
Not a performance.
Not a bargain.
A surrender.
Because your body was never meant to be the battlefield where you endlessly prove your worth.
Your worth is not earned through sexual perfection.
And your salvation is not purchased by self-discipline.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
His death and resurrection are the foundation of our hope.
Our obedience is the grateful response of those who have been redeemed.
That is why this message matters so deeply.
Somebody reading this is one decision away from returning to a relationship they know is destructive.
Somebody is about to surrender to a temptation they have resisted for weeks.
Somebody is sitting in a marriage that needs honesty and healing.
Somebody has quietly concluded that their history makes them unlovable.
And somebody has been attending church for years while believing that if people knew the truth, there would be no place left for them.
If that is you, hear the Gospel again.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the dead.
Christ calls you to repent and believe.
And everyone who truly comes to Him in faith finds a Savior whose mercy is greater than their ability to save themselves.
You are not invited to remain in bondage.
You are invited to follow Jesus into freedom.
Not freedom to do whatever desire demands.
Freedom to belong to the One who loves you with a love that is holy, sacrificial, and true.
And if this message has exposed a battle you have been fighting in silence, you do not need to publish the details of your struggle.
But you can take one honest step.
You do not have to confess private details in a public comment section. God knows what you are carrying, and trusted spiritual support can help you address what needs attention.
And if this article reached you at the right moment, consider what might happen if it reached someone else.
Someone in your family.
A friend who has drifted from church.
A young believer being taught that purity is outdated.
A married couple struggling to rebuild trust.
A person who has confused sexual shame with the voice of God.
Because faith needs more than a moment of emotion.
It needs roots.
It needs nourishment.
It needs a growing understanding of God's Word.
That is why we are continuing to build Gospel Warrior as a place where believers can be challenged, strengthened, and pointed back to Christ.
Not because God's grace can be purchased.
And certainly not because a financial contribution is required to glorify God.
But Scripture does teach that believers may voluntarily support Gospel ministry.

In Philippians 4:15–18, Paul gratefully acknowledges the financial partnership of believers who supported his work. In 2 Corinthians 9:7, he teaches that giving should be willing rather than compelled.
These are simply tangible expressions of appreciation. The greater purpose is not merchandise or membership.
It is the message.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
Sinners called to repentance.
The wounded invited to find hope in Him.
Believers equipped to grow in holiness and truth.
And a community committed to proclaiming that no human scandal is beyond the reach of God's redeeming grace.
Because this mission was never supposed to be about building an audience that admires a page.
It is about pointing people toward the Savior who changes lives.
And now, before you leave, return to the words that started everything.
“Ye are not your own.”
Maybe when you first read them, they sounded restrictive.
Like something was being taken from you.
But look at them again through the cross.
You belong to Christ.
Not to your worst mistake.
Not to the person who rejected you.
Not to the habit that has controlled you.
Not to the shame that keeps repeating your history.
If you are in Christ, you belong to the One who died for you and rose again.
And because you belong to Him, your body matters.
Your choices matter.
Your holiness matters.
Your future matters.
The Lord who calls you to turn away from sin is the Lord who gave Himself to redeem you.
So tonight, when the phone lights up...
When the old temptation returns...
When loneliness starts telling you that compromise is the only way to feel loved...
When the memory of your past whispers that you will never change...
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember whose you are.
And choose, by the grace of God, to glorify Him in your body.
Because the final word over a repentant sinner's life does not belong to the scandal.
It belongs to Jesus.
The scars of your past may still tell a story, but they do not get to write the ending when your life belongs to Christ.
